ai-at-work.title: Indian chip startup Bharat Semi lands $24M seed round as it eyes global AI sensor market
ai-at-work.excerpt: Bharat Semi says it has secured design wins for its AI-enabled sensor technology with companies including General Atomics.
ai-at-work.dwp_take: An Indian semiconductor startup called Bharat Semi just raised 24 million dollars in seed funding to develop AI sensors for global markets, and they've already lined up customers like General Atomics. This matters to digital workplace folks because the infrastructure underlying your collaboration tools, smart office spaces, and workplace IoT devices depends on chip innovation, and non-US players are finally getting serious capital. Here's the thing though: everyone's funding the next big AI thing, but most organizations still can't get basic workplace tech fundamentals right, so let's see if these sensors actually make offices smarter or just collect more useless data.

ai-at-work.title: Detectify’s Agentic Tooling lets AI agents test suspected flaws in running applications
ai-at-work.excerpt: Swedish application security company Detectify AB today launched Agentic Tooling, a set of tools aimed at letting an organization’s own artificial intelligence agents test whether suspected vulnerabil
ai-at-work.dwp_take: Detectify just released Agentic Tooling, which lets AI agents autonomously test whether suspected security vulnerabilities in live applications can actually be exploited, along with a Security Ledger to document the findings. Digital workplace teams need to care because autonomous security testing means fewer manual vulnerability checks and faster identification of real threats versus false alarms. Here's the thing though: letting AI agents loose on your production systems to find flaws is bold, and I'm genuinely curious how many organizations will actually trust it before something goes sideways.

ai-at-work.title: Agent fleets drag the messaging layer from afterthought to AI’s coordination core
ai-at-work.excerpt: Data center telemetry, sandboxed AI workloads and fleets of agents are pushing more machine-to-machine traffic through infrastructure than ever before, exposing the limits of messaging systems built f
ai-at-work.dwp_take: AI agent fleets are generating so much machine-to-machine traffic that traditional messaging systems are buckling under the load, forcing organizations to rethink their entire infrastructure stack. For digital workplace pros, this matters because the tools your employees depend on (and the backends running them) need messaging layers that can actually handle autonomous AI workloads without melting down. Here's the thing though: we've been building messaging systems for humans talking to systems for thirty years, and now we're scrambling because machines won't stop talking to each other.

ai-at-work.title: NeuralSat raises $3.2M to bring high-speed data connectivity and compute to space
ai-at-work.excerpt: German startup NeuralSat GmbH announced Thursday that it has raised €2.9 million, about $3.2 million, in pre-seed funding to develop a 72-satellite data-relay processing network aimed at speeding up t
ai-at-work.dwp_take: A German startup called NeuralSat just raised $3.2 million to build a satellite network that processes data in orbit instead of sending it all back to Earth. This matters because digital workplace infrastructure runs on connectivity, and space-based compute could eventually solve latency problems for remote teams in genuinely remote locations, not just people sitting in coffee shops. Here's the thing though: we still can't get reliable broadband to rural areas on the ground, so maybe let's fix that before we start processing cat videos in the stratosphere.

digital-culture.title: Does the workplace have a 4 p.m. problem?
digital-culture.excerpt: At 10 a.m., a meeting is just a meeting. You grab a coffee and get ready to listen to something that could probably have been summarized in an email. At 4 p.m., that same meeting can feel like a hosta
digital-culture.dwp_take: Fast Company looked at why late afternoon meetings tank productivity and morale compared to morning ones. Digital workplace managers need to pay attention here because scheduling meetings at 4 p.m. is basically asking people to mentally check out while physically present. After thirty years watching this play out, I can tell you that the real 4 p.m. problem isn't the meetings themselves, it's that we still haven't figured out that forcing knowledge workers to sit through anything after 3:30 is just theater.

digital-culture.title: Thinking of quitting your job? Don’t until you consider this factor
digital-culture.excerpt: You know that stinging sensation you get when your coworker gets the promotion that you thought was yours? Or that sinking feeling of doom when you realize that a new hire could take over your role? M
digital-culture.dwp_take: Fast Company ran a piece about how envy at work often triggers the urge to quit, suggesting people should examine this emotion before making career moves. This matters because digital workplace pros spend half their waking hours in these environments, and impulsive exits driven by social comparison cost companies real productivity and knowledge. The irony is that the person getting the promotion probably felt equally envious of someone else last week, yet here we all are, treating LinkedIn like a highlight reel and wondering why we feel behind.

industry-news.title: Ubiquiti Networks UniFi U7 Pro Max review
industry-news.excerpt: An affordable tri-band Wi-Fi 7 AP offering good performance and probably the best wireless management services in town
industry-news.dwp_take: Ubiquiti released the UniFi U7 Pro Max, a tri-band Wi-Fi 7 access point that delivers solid performance at a reasonable price point with excellent management capabilities. For digital workplace teams, this matters because reliable wireless infrastructure is the unsexy backbone that keeps remote and hybrid workers from losing their minds at 2pm on a Tuesday. At this price point with that management story, Ubiquiti just made the Wi-Fi 6 crowd look unnecessarily expensive, which is going to force some uncomfortable conversations in IT budget meetings.

industry-news.title: Can tech ever be truly circular? A rising market for refurbished hardware says it can
industry-news.excerpt: As AI drives compute demand, the confidence in pre-owned tech is proving that circular IT is a business strategy, not just an ESG target
industry-news.dwp_take: The refurbished hardware market is booming as organizations look to stretch IT budgets while chasing sustainability goals, proving there's real economic sense behind the circular economy pitch. For digital workplace teams, this means your hardware refresh cycles just got more complicated because you're now balancing performance specs against environmental impact and total cost of ownership. Here's the thing though: most organizations will embrace refurbished gear when it saves money, then pat themselves on the back for saving the planet. That's fine. Do both.

industry-news.title: Five ways CISOs can use ‘dark AI’ to their own advantage
industry-news.excerpt: Vulnerability discovery will explode over the next few years, but CIOs can use AI to beat hackers at their own game
industry-news.dwp_take: Apparently some security folks are getting excited about using AI to find vulnerabilities before the bad guys do, which is a sensible enough idea if you ignore the ominous "dark AI" branding. This matters to digital workplace pros because security theater doesn't keep anyone safe, but actual vulnerability management does, and AI tools could genuinely help identify risks faster than manual processes. That said, I've seen enough "AI will solve everything" pitches to know that the real work is still in the governance, testing, and human decision-making that no algorithm replaces, so maybe let's pump the brakes on the marketing speak first.

industry-news.title: ClickHouse expands enterprise platform with Xata acquisition
industry-news.excerpt: The expanded platform introduces new capabilities across transactional databases, observability, security, and AI engineering
industry-news.dwp_take: ClickHouse bought Xata to beef up its data platform with better transactional database support, observability tools, security features, and AI capabilities. For digital workplace folks, this matters because your employees increasingly depend on data platforms that actually work together instead of forcing IT to stitch together five different tools that hate each other. The real question is whether ClickHouse can integrate this without turning into another bloated kitchen sink that nobody asked for, but time will tell.
